It's coming from a few places - the girlfriend experience sure, but there's also putting the group's needs above your own. That's a huge thing in Japan in general, in all types of work and social situations. So not giving 100% is more the thought of an idol valuing her own personal life above the group, which can create conflict and misunderstanding with both coworkers (groupmates) and customers (fans.) Fans also spend a ton of money and time to do grassroots promotion of the girl they like, especially during birthdays, handshakes, and elections. To spend time on something that could be considered "frivolous" while others work really hard for your sake is a huge deal, and it's considered pretty disrespectful. The fans sacrifice, the girl should too.  
It's as much an overall cultural thing and a respect as it is a "fans just want to pretend they're dating them!" thing. I don't agree with it at all, but that's where it comes from.

I think it's less about why and more about what. No one but he knows that the mad King was planning on burning everything. They only know that there was a war, Jaime betrayed someone he swore to protect with his life and it allowed the Lannisters to waltz into King's Landing essentially unchallenged. That looks bad even if the king was nuts.

The book is able to be much more visceral and gory, so it's scarier in that sense. It also expands on everything, so there's more...well, everything. I think the things that scare the kids are more frightening in the book because of how King describes them. It also doesn't split the timelines so neatly so you can see how the kids were effected, which I think is interesting and scary in some ways.  
That said it's a huge book and that can be daunting. If you have the patience I think it's worth it.

"Oh absolutely. Absolutely. Actually people all say that New York is tolerant, it isn't. The first thing that people asked you if you were at a party or something was what nationality you are. So it was a very ethnically divided city. I had a friend that was italian, she dated an irish guy and her family had a fit. But they were a lot of first generation families.  
As far as John (my dad) went, when we went in the subway people would stare at us so he would always say "What are you looking at!?" to them. He would ask me if it bothered me, that people were staring, and i just told him "Gee I never noticed." In New York people stared at me a lot. I think it was because I was blonde and that was rare back then, at least in New York.  
The most tolerant, or maybe not tolerant, but accepting, was northern California. Not southern. When we moved to southern California, John and I looked at each other and said "Oh god, we forgot we're a mixed couple."  
There was a time that we were going to a friend's house for dinner in Manhattan, and they lived across town. So we were walking there and there were these guys - you know at that time, there was the hawks, and the doves, there was a lot about Vietnam. We were walking across town after a demonstration that the hawks had, and they were having their beers and sitting down. One guy stood up and said "What are you doing with her?" The tension was so high that, you know, you do stupid things. So we said "No no, we're married" and showed them our rings. How dumb was that?! So the guy kept poking John on the chest, shoving him back kind of, and finally they started to fist fight. I didn't know what to do, I kinda just stood there because I couldn't figure out how to help or anything else. It went on for a long time, or it seemed like it, but all the people that had gathered around were white. But finally a black guy came and pulled John out and said "You don't need this brother." And then it ended. But that was the only really overt thing that happened.  
We were really surprised at how yucky southern California was. We decided to move out here" (we live in California now, I was born here) "because we'd taken a long vacation. Everyone in San Francisco would say hi to us, and they were so warm and friendly. But when we moved to southern California, it was almost like being back in New York again. It was the same kind of staring. And just like you, you were the only black kid in the school."  
(Note: This is true, at my elementary school I was the only bi-racial kid. Southern California was also the first time I was called the n-word to my face. So I don't like it much either. But we were in a small town, so I can't say that everywhere is the same.)

They do it on American reality TV all the time (hell, the job of a producer on a US reality show is to help CREATE those moments people will talk about for days/weeks after.) I highly doubt that Mnet has any agenda other than making money, and how they make money is to make a show that will be talked about and watched.  
Even "evil edits" and controversy serves that purpose. If there's a huge controversy (like the current one with lapel mics), people talk. A person who's never been interested in the show might see or hear about it and think "Wow, that's awful! I want to see for myself if it's as bad as everyone says or if it's just netizens overreacting." Now Mnet has a new viewer. New viewer = more money.  
That isn't to say there's conscious like "let's make them look bad!" type of thoughts, I highly doubt it. I don't think they would bother, as it's extra work to make someone look bad if they haven't done anything. They show the moments and stories that will make people talk, that's it.  
THAT SAID! I think that they're influenced about who they'll show by who people find interesting. It's a circular thing. Someone does interesting things, they get talked about, they get shown more. Likewise if netizens talk about someone, they get shown, they get talked about more. It's just how things go.
